Mill says a public officer may **forcibly stop** a person who is about to cross an unsafe bridge when the danger is certain and there is no time to warn him; this does not infringe liberty because the person would otherwise be harmed and liberty is “doing what one desires” – he does not desire to fall into the river.  
When the danger is only a **possibility** (not certain), Mill holds that only a warning is required; the person must be allowed to decide whether to take the risk, except when he is a child, delirious, or otherwise incapable of full reflection.  
This is not a breach of liberty because the restriction is aimed at preventing harm to the individual himself, not at controlling his independent choices.  
Mill states that the principle of liberty **does not apply to children or to those who are not of full maturity** (see [3]), who must be protected against their own actions.

First edition (1859) – assumptions: breeds from age 30 to 90, produces three pairs of young (6 young) in that interval; result: after 500 years, fifteen million elephants.  
Sixth edition (1872) – assumptions: breeds from age 30 to 90, produces six young in that interval, survives to 100 years; result: after 740–750 years, nearly nineteen million elephants.  

The sixth edition increased the assumed number of offspring per breeding interval from three pairs to six young, extended the survival age, and lengthened the time span needed to reach the projected population, raising the final estimate from fifteen million to nearly nineteen million elephants.

Darwin says the struggle for existence is “the doctrine of Malthus applied … to the whole animal and vegetable kingdoms.”  
Malthus’s own essay states that population, when unchecked, increases in a **geometrical ratio**, while subsistence increases only in an **arithmetical ratio**.  
He takes the **doubling period of twenty‑five years** as the rule for unchecked population.

Mill - United States: “the feeling of the majority, to whom any appearance of a more showy or costly style of living than they can hope to rival is disagreeable, operates as a tolerably effectual sumptuary law, and that in many parts of the Union it is really difficult for a person possessing a very large income, to find any mode of spending it, which will not incur popular disapprobation.”  

Veblen - Theory of the Leisure Class: “The accepted standard of expenditure in the community or in the class to which a person belongs largely determines what his standard of living will be. It does this directly by commending itself to his common sense as right and good, through his habitually contemplating it and assimilating the scheme of life in which it belongs; but it does so also indirectly through popular insistence on conformity to the accepted scale of expenditure as a matter of propriety, under pain of disesteem and ostracism.”  

Comparison: Mill observes that majority sentiment in the U.S. acts as a social sumptuary law, discouraging ostentatious spending by the wealthy. Veblen explains this restraint as a result of the class’s internalized standard of living, where conformity to accepted expenditure patterns is enforced by social approval or disapproval. Thus, the majority’s disapproval aligns with Veblen’s idea that social conformity and the desire for status regulate consumption.
